summary: Describes NFS version 4 minor version 1, including features kept from the base protocol and extensions, such as parallel NFS. It was replaced by RFC 8881.

plainLanguage.summary: NFS version 4.1 is the Network File System protocol for sharing files over a network, published in 2010. It keeps the file system model of the earlier version 4.0 and adds sessions, directory delegations and parallel NFS, so that a request is never run twice and several storage devices can be used at once. RFC 8881 has since replaced this document.

questions: what is a delegation in nfs
subtitle: NFS version 4.1: file sharing rebuilt around sessions, exactly-once requests and parallel access to storage.

tldr.problem: NFSv4.0 had no reliable way to avoid running a request twice after a retry, handled callbacks poorly through firewalls, could not use several network paths at once, and could not spread file data over many servers.
tldr.mechanism: NFSv4.1 adds a mandatory session layer, where every request carries a SEQUENCE operation with a slot and sequence number, plus directory delegations and parallel NFS (pNFS), which hands clients layouts so they can read and write storage devices directly.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5661 has been obsoleted by RFC 8881 and was updated by RFC 8178 and RFC 8434. The abstract calls minor version 1 superior to minor version 0 and says its use is preferred.

today: RFC 5661 is obsolete: RFC 8881 replaces it, and the RFC had been updated by RFC 8178 and RFC 8434. Its status was Proposed Standard, published in January 2010.

sections.title: What NFS Version 4.1 Adds
sections.content:
The Network File System (NFS) version 4 minor version 1 is the second minor version of NFSv4. It is a separate protocol with no dependencies on NFSv4.0 (RFC 3530), so this document neither updates nor obsoletes that RFC. Both minor versions can run at the same time between the same client and server. The abstract calls minor version 1 superior to minor version 0 with no loss of functionality and says its use is preferred.

The major extensions are sessions, directory delegations and parallel NFS (pNFS). Section 1.8 also lists the RECLAIM_COMPLETE operation, attributes set atomically during exclusive create with the new EXCLUSIVE4_1 method, open files preserved after their last hard link is removed, better compatibility with Windows access control lists, data retention attributes, identification of client and server implementations, and notification when a byte-range lock may become available. LIPKEY and SPKM-3 are no longer required security mechanisms.

Minor version 1 breaks two of the minor-versioning guidelines in RFC 3530. Guideline 11 would require every client and server that supports minor version 1 also to support minor version 0, and guideline 12 forbids mandatory new features. The RFC says both divergences are forced by the sessions model and RECLAIM_COMPLETE, which are infrastructure that would add undue complexity if they were optional.
sections.plainLanguage: NFS version 4.1 is a full version of the NFS file-sharing protocol in its own right. It works alongside the earlier version 4.0 and adds sessions, directory delegations and parallel data access to storage devices.

sections.title: COMPOUND: Many Operations in One Request
sections.content:
NFSv4.1 is a Remote Procedure Call (RPC) application that uses RPC version 2 and the External Data Representation (XDR) encoding. In every NFSv4 minor version there are exactly two RPC procedures, NULL and COMPOUND. A COMPOUND request is a series of individual operations, such as LOOKUP, GETATTR, OPEN and READ, that do the work of the traditional NFS procedures.

The server evaluates the operations in order, with no atomicity guarantee. When one operation fails, evaluation stops and the results of everything evaluated so far go back to the client. Chaining several LOOKUP operations for a multi-component path, or combining OPEN with READ, removes extra round trips.

Unlike NFSv3, which used ancillary protocols such as NLM, NSM and MOUNT, all NFSv4 minor versions use this single RPC protocol. Locking is integrated, and the work of MOUNT is done by LOOKUP from a per-server global root filehandle. The server can also call the client: there are two callback procedures, CB_NULL and CB_COMPOUND, built the same way. New operations can be added inside COMPOUND, which is how minor versions extend the protocol. Except for a small number of session-creation operations, all requests run inside a session.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of sending one small request per operation, the client sends a list of operations in a single COMPOUND procedure. The server works down the list in order and stops at the first failure.

sections.title: RPC Security and Kerberos
sections.content:
Older NFS relied on host-based trust: the server trusted the client machine to vouch for its users, and AUTH_SYS carried only a user identity. NFSv4.1 clients and servers MUST implement RPCSEC_GSS, which uses the GSS-API to provide per-request authentication, integrity checking and, optionally, privacy. Implementing it is required; using it is not, so AUTH_SYS may still be used but is only an OPTIONAL flavor and interoperability through it is not assured.

Both sides MUST support the authentication and integrity services. Servers MUST support the privacy service and clients SHOULD. Both MUST support the Kerberos V5 mechanism with a quality of protection of zero, which lets the mechanism decide the protection level. The server identifies itself with a host-based service name of the form service@hostname, where the service is nfs; for Kerberos the form nfs/hostname is RECOMMENDED.

The RFC does not name the required Kerberos algorithms. It says implementors should track the Kerberos standard, and that real security depends on the existing Kerberos infrastructure. At the time of writing, AES with HMAC-SHA1 was a REQUIRED algorithm set for Kerberos V5, whereas NFSv4.0 had to require weaker sets.
sections.plainLanguage: Every request and reply can be authenticated, checked for changes and encrypted. The protocol requires implementations to support Kerberos V5 through RPCSEC_GSS. The older host-based AUTH_SYS method is optional.

sections.title: Sessions, Channels and Trunking
sections.content:
Sessions fix four shortcomings the RFC lists for earlier NFS: no exactly-once semantics, limited callback support (no callbacks through firewalls, and races between replies and callbacks), limited trunking over multiple network paths, and a need for machine credentials for fully secure operation. NFSv4.1 clients and servers MUST support and MUST use sessions.

A session is a long-lived server object that a client creates and then uses from one or more transport connections. A single client may create several sessions, but one session MUST NOT serve more than one client. Locking state such as locks, delegations and layouts is tied to the client ID (a 64-bit identifier), not to any session, so a callback can arrive on a different session from the one that acquired the state. Each time a session is used, whether by a request or by the client answering a callback, the state leased to its client ID is renewed.

Each session has a fore channel for client requests and may have a backchannel for server callbacks. The client creates the transport connections and gives them to the server, which solves the firewall problem, because callbacks travel back over connections the client controls. A connection can carry one channel or both, and the client can attach any number of connections.

Trunking uses several connections at once to increase transfer speed. Session trunking associates multiple connections with one session. Client ID trunking associates multiple sessions with one client ID; the server then coordinates locking state across those sessions. Servers MUST support both forms within the set of network addresses used to access a single server, and clustered servers MAY allow client ID trunking across different servers that share locking state.

Setup runs through EXCHANGE_ID and then CREATE_SESSION. Establishing identification by a new incarnation of a client also releases locking state held by the previous incarnation. A client that wants delegations, layouts or directory notifications must make sure a backchannel exists, using BIND_CONN_TO_SESSION if needed, and tells the server what callback security it accepts through BACKCHANNEL_CTL.
sections.plainLanguage: A session is a standing arrangement between one client and one server. The client opens one or more network connections and hands them to the server, so server callbacks travel back through connections the client controls. Several connections can carry the same session, which spreads traffic across network paths.

sections.title: Exactly Once Semantics and the Reply Cache
sections.content:
Every COMPOUND that starts with a SEQUENCE operation MUST be executed exactly once, on both the fore channel and the backchannel, whether or not reply caching was requested. The RFC explains why even idempotent requests need this. A repeated RENAME gives a wrong error. A repeated WRITE can corrupt data: a slow first copy can still be waiting in the server's I/O system when the retry has already been answered and a later overlapping write has been sent, and then the late first copy overwrites the newer data.

Old NFS duplicate caches were keyed on the 32-bit RPC transaction ID (XID) and replaced entries by least recently used order, so they were never complete. NFSv4.1 instead uses a slot table. The requester picks an unused slot ID in the range 0 to N, where N starts as ca_maxrequests minus 1 and can be adjusted by SEQUENCE replies. Each slot holds a sequence ID and the cached reply for the request sent with it.

The sequence ID is a 32-bit unsigned value. The first use of a slot MUST use sequence ID one, and every reuse MUST use one greater than the last, wrapping from 0xFFFFFFFF to zero. If the received sequence ID equals the one recorded for the slot, the server returns the cached reply instead of running the request again. A sequence ID that is less than the recorded one, or two or more greater, produces NFS4ERR_SEQ_MISORDERED. Because the number of outstanding requests is bounded by the slot table, the cache has a bounded size and can be kept in stable storage. Complete exactly-once behavior is only possible when the server persists the reply cache and never needs to restart.
sections.plainLanguage: If a reply is lost, the client sends the same request again. The server tracks each request with a slot number and a sequence number, and if it has already answered that request it returns the saved answer instead of running the request twice.

sections.title: State, Stateids, Leases and Recovery
sections.content:
NFSv4 is stateful. When the server grants a lock of any kind, it returns a stateid, a 128-bit value that stands for that lock or set of locks. A stateid is always interpreted against the client ID of the current session, and it may be used on any session of that client ID. The kinds of state are share reservations established by OPEN, byte-range locks, file delegations, directory delegations and layouts.

All of a client's state shares one lease. Each time a session is used, the state leased to its client ID is renewed for the period given by the lease_time attribute. If the client stops renewing, the server may release its locks once the lease expires, so a crashed client does not block others forever. A server MAY keep a session inactivity timer, and that timer MUST NOT be shorter than lease_time.

After a server restart, or after locking state is lost in some other way, clients discover it through errors such as NFS4ERR_BADSESSION, NFS4ERR_DEADSESSION or NFS4ERR_STALE_CLIENTID. They then recreate a session or a new client ID and reclaim their locks during a special grace period, using reclaim-type requests. The RECLAIM_COMPLETE operation tells the server that the client has finished reclaiming. When a client reclaims a delegation after a server restart, the server grants it but marks it as recalled, so the client must write its modified state to the server and then return it. Layouts are an exception: unlike other locking state, they are not reclaimed.
sections.plainLanguage: The server gives the client a 128-bit stateid for each lock it grants. All of a client's locks share one lease. As long as the client keeps using its session, the lease stays alive; if the client stops, the server may give the locks to other clients. After a server restart, clients reclaim their locks during a grace period.

sections.title: Delegations and Client-Side Caching
sections.content:
NFSv4.1 does not provide distributed cache coherence. It defines a limited set of caching guarantees so that locks and share reservations work without destructive interference from client-side caches. A delegation passes part of the server's job to a client, so the client can decide open and close questions locally while no other client conflicts. The server recalls the delegation with a callback when another client needs the file. The server does not delegate until it has tested the backchannel with a CB_COMPOUND containing a single CB_SEQUENCE operation, and clients MUST NOT assume that any particular open will produce a delegation.

There are two kinds of open delegation. OPEN_DELEGATE_READ lets several clients hold read delegations at the same time without conflict; the holder is assured that the contents, most attributes and the names of links to the file will not change without its knowledge. OPEN_DELEGATE_WRITE is exclusive, so the holder may modify data locally; only one may exist for a file at a time, and it conflicts with all read delegations. The server may recall a delegation whenever it wants, and changes made through other protocols or local access that would break the guarantee must also cause a recall. If the client does not answer the recall, the server revokes the delegation, and the client finds out the next time it uses the delegation's stateid.

Delegation recovery deals with client restart, server restart and network partition. After a server restart, delegations are reclaimed like locks, but with the recalled designation described above. NFSv4.1 also adds directory delegations, an OPTIONAL feature requested with GET_DIR_DELEGATION. They are read-only and cover the directory's attributes and its entries. A client may ask for asynchronous notifications of changes instead of a recall each time, which helps with very large or slowly changing directories and with workloads that often look up names that do not exist, such as compiling software. Directory delegations are not reclaimed after a restart; the client simply asks again.
sections.plainLanguage: A delegation lets the server promise a client that no other client will open or change a file, so the client can cache the file without asking the server each time. If another client needs the file, the server calls back and asks for the delegation to be returned.

sections.title: A Namespace Across Servers
sections.content:
A server presents all its exports as a single tree reachable from a per-server global root filehandle, so a client can browse with LOOKUP and READDIR and no MOUNT protocol is needed. Where parts of the path are not exported, the server bridges the gap with a read-only pseudo file system that shows only exported directories. Each pseudo file system MUST have its own fsid, unique on that server. The RFC's example is /a as pseudo, /a/b as real, /a/b/c as pseudo and /a/b/c/d as real. Pseudo file systems are usually built when the server starts, so their filehandles are often volatile and clients must be ready to recover them after NFS4ERR_FHEXPIRED.

Across servers, the location attributes fs_locations and fs_locations_info record where instances of a file system can be found. When a file system is present, those attributes give alternative locations to use if the current one becomes unavailable, which the RFC calls replication. When a present file system becomes absent, continued access returns NFS4ERR_MOVED and the client follows the successor locations, which the RFC calls migration. A location that was never present and exists only through its location record is a referral, which lets one server place a file system that lives on another server inside its own namespace. The protocol does not specify how a server moves a file system; it only specifies how the client is told.

Client support for location attributes is OPTIONAL, so a server may hide migration and referral events from such clients by acting as a proxy. The fs_locations_info attribute can give each location a priority and can say whether locations may be used at the same time, and it can include variables the client fills in so that different clients are sent to different file systems.
sections.plainLanguage: A server presents all of its exports as one folder tree. Location records let that tree continue on other servers: a client can be pointed to a file system on another server, switch to a replica, or follow a file system that has moved.

sections.title: Parallel NFS (pNFS)
sections.content:
Parallel NFS (pNFS) is an OPTIONAL feature that splits file service in two. A metadata server handles names, attributes and permissions, while clients read and write file data straight to storage devices, which may be multiple and higher-throughput compared with the server alone. The data path uses a storage protocol chosen by the layout type: NFSv4.1 itself (the file layout type in Section 13), a block or volume protocol such as iSCSI, or an object protocol. Control between the metadata server and the storage devices is outside the scope of the RFC. A pNFS server MUST still support normal NFSv4.1 access to every file it exposes through pNFS, so a client without a matching storage protocol keeps working.

The key object is the layout, which maps a byte range of a file to the storage devices that hold the data. A layout belongs to a layout type that defines the storage protocol. Layouts are leased, recallable and revocable, like data delegations, but they are separate objects manipulated with new operations such as LAYOUTGET and LAYOUTCOMMIT. A client must hold a layout before it sends I/O to a storage device. The file layout type stripes data across NFSv4.1 data servers, both file by file and, inside large files, block by block.

The normal flow starts when the client meets a new file system and asks for the fs_layout_type attribute. If it has no client ID that was granted the pNFS metadata server role, it sends EXCHANGE_ID with EXCHGID4_FLAG_USE_PNFS_MDS set, creates a session, opens the file and reads its layout type with GETATTR. LAYOUTGET, using the filehandle and stateid from the open, returns a layout that may cover only part of the requested range, together with device IDs and a description of how data is organized across the devices. GETDEVICEINFO maps a device ID to device addresses, the client sends I/O with the chosen storage protocol, and those requests may run in parallel to several devices. After a write, LAYOUTCOMMIT reports the new size and modification time to the metadata server.
sections.plainLanguage: In parallel NFS, one server keeps the names and permissions while clients read and write the file data directly on storage devices. A layout tells the client which device holds each part of a file, so one client can use several devices at the same time.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC calls the old authentication model unsafe: the server trusted the client machine, and AUTH_SYS simply named the end user. NFSv4.1 implementations are REQUIRED to support end-to-end authentication, in which a user on a client mutually authenticates with a principal on the server through cryptographic schemes that do not expose passwords or keys in the clear. Being required to implement does not mean required to use, but AUTH_SYS is only an OPTIONAL flavor, so interoperability through it is not assured.

Users may decline integrity protection for speed, which leaves a man-in-the-middle able to modify requests and replies. Three cases deserve protection regardless of user choice. SECINFO and SECINFO_NO_NAME are RECOMMENDED to be sent with an integrity-protecting flavor, because their results tell the client which security mechanisms to use and an attacker could otherwise push the client toward a weaker option. Any GETATTR for fs_locations or fs_locations_info SHOULD also use integrity protection, to stop an attacker faking NFS4ERR_MOVED and then redirecting the client to a server the attacker controls.

NFSv4.1 adds further security considerations for pNFS, for locking and session state, for state reclaim during the grace period, and for the SSV-based state protection of RPCSEC_GSS. The impact of pNFS on security depends on the storage protocol and can be as low as zero.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol expects strong end-to-end authentication instead of trust in the client machine. It also warns that three operations, which decide security settings and file system locations, should always be protected against modification in transit.
